name: DAILY Pinterest Posts 5:45PM
instructions:
Write 10 Pinterest titles and descriptions, each a summary of a story from today's daily data files. Rank them best to worst. ASSIGN EACH POST TO A SPECIFIC BOARD. Save the posts to a text file. Attach the file to an email and send it to hello@phantom-byte.com. AFTER the task is complete and email has been sent, message me on Telegram saying, "Email sent with today's Pinterest posts."

IMPORTANT: Your final response is what gets delivered to Telegram. It must contain ONLY the words "Email sent with today's Pinterest posts" and nothing else. Do not include the posts, a summary, a report, or any other content in your final response. The posts go in the email only.

Load the writing-style skill before generating the posts. Apply every rule in it.

Pinterest limits: title max 100 chars, description max 500 chars. Write each description targeting 350-400 chars from the start so they fit under 500 without trimming. Use keyword-rich descriptions for Pinterest SEO.

HARD RULE — POSTS ARE SUMMARIES OF THE STORY, NOT GENERIC EVERGREEN CLICKBAIT (CRITICAL): Every post MUST summarize a specific, concrete story pulled from today's data files. Lead with the actual who, what, and number from that story. Do NOT write canned textbook definitions like "This evergreen guide explains...", "What Is X?", or "How X Works" that could apply to any day. A post that does not name a real story, a real company, a real model, or a real number from the data is a FAILURE. The reader must be able to tell exactly which news story the pin is about. If the story is a tutorial or explainer, summarize what the tutorial actually teaches and tie it to the specific event or trend that makes it relevant today, not a generic definition. NEVER open a post with "This evergreen guide..." or "What Is...".

THE 7 BOARDS (assign every post to exactly one of these, by name):
1. Main AI News
2. AI Agents
3. AI Tools
4. AI for Developers
5. Agent Security
6. Robotics & Physical AI
7. Quantum Computing

Match each story to the board whose topic fits it best. A story about an AI agent goes on "AI Agents", a security/prompt-injection story goes on "Agent Security", a robotics story goes on "Robotics & Physical AI", a quantum story goes on "Quantum Computing", a developer/programming story goes on "AI for Developers", a business/productivity tool story goes on "AI Tools", and general AI news goes on "Main AI News". Spread posts across boards sensibly — do not put all 10 on one board.

PINTEREST TREND CHECK — MANDATORY EVERY RUN, AND IT MUST SHAPE THE POSTS (CRITICAL):
After reading the data files, and BEFORE writing any post, you must check live Pinterest trend data and use it to decide which stories to post and how to word them.
Step A: From the stories you have shortlisted, write a list of 15 to 25 candidate Pinterest search phrases — the phrase a real Pinterest user would type for that story's topic (for example "humanoid robot", "cybersecurity", "smart home", "drone", "ai news"). One phrase per shortlisted story, plus close variants where useful. Use plain, human search phrasing, not headline phrasing.
Step B: Run this exact command (one terminal call) with your phrases, comma-separated, and read the whole output:
    python3 ~/.hermes/scripts/pinterest_trends.py --terms "phrase one,phrase two,phrase three"
Step C: Read the four trend lists it prints (SEASONAL, POPULAR, BREAKOUT, TRENDING SEARCHES) and the KEYWORD DEMAND block.
Step D: Use the output in three ways, and only these three ways:
    1. STORY CHOICE — when two candidate stories are similarly strong, prefer the one whose keyword phrase the script reports (it has measurable Pinterest search volume), and prefer RISING over FLAT over FALLING.
    2. KEYWORD PLACEMENT — put that reported phrase in the pin title and in the first ~50 characters of the description, since Pinterest reads those first. The phrase must be one the script actually returned, or a natural variant of it.
    3. SEASONAL ANGLE — if a SEASONAL or BREAKOUT list term honestly describes the story's own subject, use that phrasing in the description keywords. If it does not honestly describe the story, ignore it.
The trend check may shape which stories you pick and which words you use. It may NEVER be used to claim something the data does not say. Do not state a trend percentage in a post. Do not write that anything is "trending on Pinterest". Do not bolt a seasonal term onto an unrelated story.
If a story's phrases return no Pinterest volume, that is a real answer: no demand signal. You may still post that story, but write it plainly with no trend or seasonality angle.
Never skip this step and never claim you ran it without running it.

SPACING REQUIREMENT (CRITICAL — MUST FOLLOW EXACTLY): The file and email body MUST have a BLANK LINE between every title and its description, AND a BLANK LINE between every post. Do NOT run title lines, description lines, and posts together into a wall of text. The exact required format for each post is:
[BOARD NAME] - Post title
<blank line>
Description text
<blank line>
Then the next post begins. Always end the description with a blank line before the next [BOARD NAME] line. There must never be a description line directly followed by the next post's [BOARD NAME] line with no blank line between them, and never a title line directly followed by its description with no blank line. Use the literal newline "\n\n" (two newlines) to create each blank line.

THE EMAIL MUST SHOW THE BOARD ASSIGNMENT. Format the email body (not just the attachment) so each post is listed EXACTLY as above with the blank-line spacing:
[BOARD NAME] - Post title
<blank line>
Description text
<blank line>
The email body must clearly state which board each post goes on. Do not send an email that lists posts without their board.

CRITICAL EXECUTION ORDER — DO NOT DEVIATE:
Step 1: Read ALL the data files (one read_file or terminal call per file). There are MULTIPLE data files in today's folder — for example 20-AI-News-Stories-YYYY-MM-DD.md, tensorfeed_report_YYYY-MM-DD.txt, blogwatcher-dump-YYYY-MM-DD.txt, and ironpulse-YYYY-MM-DD.txt. Read every one of them. Do not stop after the first file. The data files contain far more stories than you need — you only need 10, so there is always enough fresh material.
Step 2: PRE-WRITE DEDUP CHECK — run this exact terminal command with NO arguments BEFORE writing any posts:
    python3 ~/.hermes/scripts/pinterest_dedup.py
    This fetches and prints every title already pinned on all 7 boards. Read its output carefully and note which stories are already pinned. You MUST know what is already pinned before you write a single post.
Step 3: PINTEREST TREND CHECK — run the trend script described in the PINTEREST TREND CHECK section above with 15 to 25 candidate phrases built from your shortlisted stories, and read its full output before writing anything.
Step 4: Write 10 posts in a single write_file call, each tagged with its assigned board, and EACH FOLLOWING THE SPACING REQUIREMENT ABOVE (blank line between title and description, blank line between posts). Write posts ONLY about stories that are NOT already pinned. DIG DEEP: go through ALL the data files you read in Step 1 and pick 10 distinct stories that are NOT already pinned. If a candidate story is already pinned, SKIP it and keep looking through the data files for a different story that is not pinned. There are many more stories in the data files than 10, so you can always find 10 that are not already pinned. Do not give up after the first few stories. Write them SHORT from the start, targeting 350-400 chars per description so they fit under 500 without trimming. REMEMBER: each post must summarize a specific story from the data, not a generic evergreen definition, and the trend check from Step 3 must have informed the story picks and the keywords.
Step 5: HARD CHARACTER GATE. Run ONE execute_code call that programmatically prints the character count of EVERY title (limit 100) and EVERY description (limit 500) in the file you just wrote, and the number of violations. If ANY post is over either limit, REWRITE THAT POST SHORT FROM SCRATCH (write a fresh 380 to 420 char description, NEVER trim an over-long draft down) and overwrite the file, then run the check again. Repeat until one check reports ZERO violations. This gate is the ONLY thing allowed to delay the email. Do NOT proceed to Step 6 while any post is over a limit.
Step 6: HARD DEDUP GATE — run this exact terminal command, passing the path to the posts file you just wrote:
    python3 ~/.hermes/scripts/pinterest_dedup.py ~/pinterest_posts_YYYY-MM-DD.txt
    (replace YYYY-MM-DD with today's date). This script fetches the live already-pinned titles from all 7 boards and REMOVES any post that duplicates a story already pinned. It rewrites the file in place. Whatever survives is what you email. Do NOT re-add removed posts. If the script removes posts, that is correct — email the survivors.
Step 7: Send the email with the surviving file attached using the email-sender skill (terminal call to the SMTP script). THE EMAIL IS THE PRIMARY DELIVERABLE, and the Step 5 character gate must have reported ZERO violations first. Never email a post over a limit, never email a post whose title is over 100 chars. If a story will not fit, replace it with a different story from the data files rather than shipping an over-limit post. The email body MUST list each post with its assigned board, WITH the blank-line spacing.
Step 8: Your final response must be ONLY "Email sent with today's Pinterest posts."

FALLBACK RULE — AN EMPTY EMAIL IS NEVER ACCEPTABLE, AND EVERGREEN IS A LAST RESORT:
The data files contain many more stories than 10, so in practice you will almost always find 10 fresh news stories that are not already pinned. Only fall back to evergreen educational posts if you have genuinely read ALL the data files and EVERY single story in them is already pinned — this should be extremely rare. If that truly happens, do NOT email an empty file. Instead, write 10 fresh posts on foundational AI topics that are NOT already pinned, and give each one a fresh, current angle tied to a specific story or trend in today's data (for example, explain a concept through a recent real-world example or a current event) rather than a stale textbook definition. Assign each to the best-fitting board. These posts must not duplicate anything already pinned. They must ALSO follow the blank-line spacing requirement. Then proceed through the remaining steps and email the file. The posts file must always contain 10 non-duplicate posts before emailing.

HARD RULES:
- Use execute_code for the Step 5 character gate and for nothing else. Run it, fix every violation, re-run until it reports zero. That is expected work, not a loop.
- The email MUST be sent. It is non-negotiable. Never skip it, and never send it carrying a post over a character limit.
- CHARACTER LIMITS ARE HARD: title 100 chars max, description 500 chars max. Pinterest silently truncates over-limit text. A post over either limit is rewritten SHORT from scratch, never trimmed, and never emailed over the limit.
- Do NOT loop on anything except the Step 5 character gate.
- Do NOT claim the email was sent unless you actually ran the SMTP script and it returned success. If the email fails, say so honestly in your final response.
- EVERY post MUST have a board assignment. A post with no board is a failure.
- The pre-write dedup check in Step 2 is MANDATORY. Run it before writing any posts.
- The Pinterest trend check in Step 3 is MANDATORY. Run the script, read the output, and let it steer story choice and keywords. Never state a trend number in a post and never claim a trend that the script did not report.
- The dedup gate in Step 6 is MANDATORY. Run it before emailing. Do not skip it.
- The posts file must NEVER be empty when emailed. If all news is already pinned, use the evergreen fallback.
- PREFER FRESH NEWS STORIES OVER EVERGREEN. Dig through all the data files for non-duplicate news before ever considering evergreen posts.
- The blank-line spacing requirement in this prompt is MANDATORY for every post in both the file and the email body.
- NO GENERIC EVERGREEN CLICKBAIT. Every post must summarize a specific story from today's data files. Never open with "This evergreen guide..." or "What Is...".

name: MONEY MAKING IDEAS TO USE INSTABOX.SH
instructions:
Find 7 Small Business Opportunities Using Instabox.sh

Objective

I want to identify practical, profitable ways to use my new Instabox.sh server to solve real problems for small businesses.

1. Research the available resources

Start by reading and analyzing the data: "C:\Users\<user>\OneDrive\Desktop\TODAYS DATA FILES"

Use that information to identify potential business problems, unmet needs, inefficient processes, and opportunities to build useful solutions.

Next, research Instabox.sh directly. Examine its website, documentation, available features, and API capabilities. We already have API access, so inspect what’s available to determine exactly what the server can and cannot do.

## IMPORTANT: DO NOT MAKE THIS A REPORT ABOUT WHAT THE BOX IS OR ISN'T, I ALREADY KNOW WHAT IT IS. i WANT YOU TO RESEARCH IS SO YOU KNOW AND DO NOT BLINDLY RECCOMEND OPPORTUNITIES. 

Important: API ACCESS IS READ-ONLY FOR THIS TASK. You may inspect endpoints, configurations, capabilities, and available resources, but do not create, modify, deploy, delete, start, stop, or otherwise change anything on the server.

Do not assume capabilities that you cannot verify. Clearly distinguish confirmed capabilities from anything that would require additional development or services.

2. Identify 7 money-making opportunities

Come up with 7 practical business opportunities that use Instabox.sh to solve problems small businesses actually experience and would pay to have fixed.

Possible solutions could include:

Customizable applications that businesses can call directly or connect to their existing agent infrastructure through MCP or APIs.
Web-based tools that perform specific business functions through MCP or API integrations.
Business dashboards and monitoring tools.
Custom workflows that automate repetitive, expensive, or inefficient business processes.
Specialized tools that solve a specific problem for a particular industry.

These are examples, not limitations. Explore other possibilities.

3. Selection criteria

Every idea must meet these criteria:

Solve a specific, recognizable problem.
Address a problem that costs a business time, money, or customers.
Be simple enough for a business owner to understand immediately.
Have a clear reason why a business would pay for the solution.
Be realistic to build and operate using Instabox.sh and the resources available.
Have a relatively low implementation and operating cost.
Avoid oversaturated ideas that countless developers and companies are already selling.

Prioritize overlooked problems and underserved business niches rather than trying to compete in crowded markets.

4. Present each opportunity

For each of the 7 ideas, provide:

1. Product or service: A simple name and explanation of what it does.

2. The problem: Exactly what business problem it solves.

3. Target industries: Identify the specific industries and types of businesses most likely to need it. Explain why they would benefit.

4. Why they would pay: Explain the business value and what makes the problem worth paying to solve.

5. How Instabox.sh is used: Explain exactly how the server, its capabilities, APIs, and integrations would power the solution.

6. Implementation guide: Provide a straightforward, step-by-step guide to building the solution, from the initial setup to a working product.

7. Revenue opportunity: Suggest a realistic way to charge for it, such as a monthly subscription, setup fee, usage-based pricing, or another appropriate model.

5. Final requirements

Rank the 7 opportunities by their practicality and commercial potential.

Keep the explanations straightforward. Focus on products and services that can realistically be built, marketed, and sold to small businesses.

Do not turn this into an elaborate business plan or overengineer the solutions.

The goal is simple: find overlooked business problems, build inexpensive solutions using Instabox.sh, and create products or services that small businesses will actually pay for.

When done. Add the well-formatted text document/report to the following file using the date to create unique file names, and add them here: "C:\Users\<user>\OneDrive\Desktop\MONEY MAKING OPPORTUNITIES"

AFTER that, email me the report using the email sender skill by attaching the text report to the email, and ginvg me a summary of the report. THEN notify me on tellingram that the email has been sent.

name: SOCIAL MEDIA QUESTIONS - 5PM
instructions:
Go look at the following data files, (Data file: C:\Users\<user>\OneDrive\Desktop\TODAYS DATA FILES) THEN find me 10 great social media posts I can post on X, which are related to today's AI news. Rank them from best to worst. For each post, include a 1-2 sentence explanation of why it's a good post. Save the posts to a text file. Attach the file to an email and send it to hello@phantom-byte.com. AFTER the task is complete and email has been sent, message me on Telegram saying, "Social media questions are ready."

IMPORTANT: Your final response is what gets delivered to Telegram. It must contain ONLY the words "Social media questions are ready" and nothing else. Do not include the posts, a summary, a report, or any other content in your final response. The posts go in the email only.

THESE POSTS MUST BE BASED ON THE DATA AND SHOULD NOT BE THE SAME EVERY DAY. MAKE THEM ENGAGING AND FUN.

VOICE AND FRAMING (READ THIS FIRST, IT OVERRIDES ANYTHING ELSE):
These posts must reflect MY actual views. My position is: I think AI SAVES us, not dooms us. It is a tool that gives people leverage, an escape route, with no permission and no gatekeeper. The architect who builds owns the leverage, not the person chasing the latest weight. So the DEFAULT tone across the batch is positive, optimistic, factual, and pro-builder.

BUT: I am not naive. If the data genuinely contains a real doom story, a real loss, a real setback that is verifiable and material, you are allowed to cover it honestly as what it is. Do not whitewash a genuinely bad event into a win, and do not force a happy spin on it. The rule is: most posts should be positive and optimistic, because that is my honest view of AI's direction, but a genuine doom story gets told straight when it is real.

What you must NEVER do:
- NEVER manufacture doom where there is none. Do not take a non-doom story (a capability jump, a cost inversion, a business move, a common growing-pain failure) and twist it into fear-mongering. That is doom porn. Do not spin mishaps (agents gaffing a test, robots bursting into flames, shopping agents erring) into "AI is dangerous" or "progress is hype." Those are normal growing pains of a young field, state the messy part plainly and move on.
- NEVER use the banned fear hooks even on a real doom story: no job-loss bait ("what does that do to your job" / "your job is gone"), no "who loses here" / "humans are being replaced by the models they trained" laments, no "AI is not safe to deploy," no "the real product is the user" cynicism about companies monetizing, no "builders admit they overshot." A real doom story is reported as a fact, not as a panic sermon.
- NEVER oversell. No "changes everything," no "revolutionary," no "the future is here," no claiming a capability is further along than the data says, no calling a company move a guaranteed winner. Optimism must be earned and grounded in a concrete, verifiable fact. No cheerleading.
- Never end a post by inviting a reply about fear, doom, or despair. Even a genuine doom story ends on a clear-eyed note, not a plea.

THE FRAMING I WANT, per story type:
- Capability jumps (Anthropic agents, Gemini video, cheaper/faster models): state the concrete fact, then what it now lets a builder do. Positive and factual. Not "what does that do to a human," not "the end of humans," not "this saves the world."
- Cost inversions (AI cheaper than humans at a task): frame as: this is why you learn to build and own systems. The people who rent intelligence or chase weights lose, but the builders gain leverage. State it as fact, do not oversell. That is the take, not "your job."
- Incidents and failures (agents gaffing a test, robots on fire, MTurk shutting down): frame as normal growing pains of a young field, early bugs being ironed out, exactly what happens when anything is built fast. Not doom. Not "everything is perfect," but not a fear story either. Progress has a messy middle, say the messy part plainly.
- Business moves (Nvidia buying HF, OpenAI ads): frame as the game, the economics, the chess move. Sharp and factual. A $13B bid is evidence open source is the center of gravity, stated as a fact, not a hallelujah.
- Genuine doom, when the data really has one (a real shutdown, a real loss, a real setback that is verifiable and material): report it straight as the factual event it is, no spin, no whitewash, no panic, no fear bait. One such post in a batch is fine and honest. It should not dominate; the default is positive.
- My signature rhetorical move (from writing-style skill): take a hype phrase the crowd parrots and invert it into a real point about building and owning leverage. "Open source so back? It never left. You chase weights. You rent intelligence. The people building architecture own the leverage. Stop chasing models. Start building systems." Use this move where it fits naturally; do not force it.

The questions you end posts with must invite the reader toward a reply about building, using, choosing, or a genuine open question in that spirit. They must never invite doom replies and never invite hype back-slapping. You are the guy who built the machine. Write like it.

Load both writing-style and x-algorithm-post-optimization skills before generating the posts. Apply every rule in both skills, especially the REAL weight values from the Aug 13 2026 release of home-mixer/params/param.rs.

Optimize for the algorithm's top signals in this priority order:
1. SHARE VIA COPY LINK (weight 20.0, the #1 signal): make at least 3 of the 10 posts forwardable frameworks or self-contained statements someone would copy-paste to a specific friend or group. Named frameworks, checklists, or "send this to someone building X" content.
2. MUTUAL REPLIES (weight 5.0 x 15.0 bidirectional boost = 75 effective, the single highest-value engagement): make at least 4 of the 10 posts end in a question or stake that invites a reply from someone who follows you back. A question the reader feels compelled to answer beats one that answers itself. The questions must be in the clear-eyed builder spirit, not doom and not hype.
3. QUOTE and SHARE VIA DM (weight 5.0 each): make posts self-contained and quotable, worth sending to one specific person.
4. FOLLOW AUTHOR (weight 4.0): signal a consistent angle worth following.
5. FAVORITE (weight 0.5, the floor): concrete, verifiable facts.

Minimize the catastrophic negatives: P(report) -234, P(mute_author) -58.8, P(not_interested) -47.52, P(block_author) -31.2. No bait-and-switch hooks, no personal attacks, no spammy cliches.

Use specific named entities (company names, model names, person names, paper titles) so the post is topically retrievable by the Phoenix two-tower model. Vary the angle, target, and domain across all 10 posts to satisfy the Author Diversity Scorer (each post after the first in a batch is decayed by 0.5).

POST FORMAT, MANDATORY. Each post is FOUR stanzas separated by blank lines, never one compressed line:
1. HOOK, one short line, 3 to 6 words. A verdict or a stake, never a topic label. Nothing else on that line.
2. FACT STANZA, one dense paragraph. Name the real entity, then the hard specifics from the data: numbers, versions, licenses, who built it, what changed.
3. TAKE, one line. The opinion stated plainly, then the one real question, and the question must invite a reply about building, choosing, or using.
4. CLOSER, one short line. A blunt contrast that lands the point. A statement, never a second question.

NAMED ENTITIES AND TRENDING TERMS, HARD RULE, added October 7, 2026. Read this BEFORE writing and apply it to every post in the batch:
Every post must name its actual subject and carry the exact terms the audience is already typing, searching, and arguing about. A post with no named entity has nothing for a reader to search, nothing to forward, and nothing for the Phoenix two-tower retrieval model to match against a user embedding, so it is invisible.
- Name the subject in the first two lines. If the subject is Grok Bot, write "Grok Bot." Never "this feature," "this tool," "the announcement," or any pronoun standing in for a name the reader has to guess.
- Keep every proper noun, product name, and number from the source story. In the October 7, 2026 case that produced this rule, the required vocabulary was Grok Bot, Opus 5.5, Midjourney, SpaceXAI, and Elon, and all of them belonged in the post. Stripping them to sound neutral produced a post that was rejected with "This post says nothing about grokbot, SpaceX nothing, WTF?"
- The opinion rides on top of the facts, never replaces them. Naming the entity, the model, and the number is the first job. The take is the second job. A post with a strong opinion and no proper nouns is a post about nothing.
- Neutrality is not a reason to strip a name. State the fact stanza factually and plainly, then make the point that is actually mine. Naming a company is not attacking it, and the report and mute weights are triggered by targeting people, not by naming products.
- Test every post before shipping: read it with all proper nouns removed. If what remains could be about any product released in the last year, the post failed and gets rewritten with the names put back in.

LENGTH: 150 to 280 characters per post, hard ceiling 280 (the free-account limit). The 190-character limit applies to the separate Social Media Questions batch ONLY. Never compress a post to fit 190.

PUNCTUATION, HARD RULE: never use a dash as punctuation to join two clauses. No em dashes, no hyphens standing in for one, and no line-level dash connecting two thoughts. This was rejected before. Write two sentences, or use a colon, a comma, or a period.

ANTI-GENERIC RULE: this batch must NOT read like the last one. Vary the opening move, the stanza count, and the target across the set. A batch where every post opens on a short verdict, runs a colon fact list, asks a question, and ends on a contrast reads as formula, and formula is what gets called generic trash. Change the shape per post. Cover different companies, models, and story types. If a post could have been written any day from any data, cut it.

SELF-CONTAINED: a stranger who has never seen the account must understand the post with no context, and every post carries the vocabulary the audience actually uses.

FINAL VOICE CHECK BEFORE YOU SEND: Read each post out loud twice. First pass: does any post read as doom porn, manufactured fear, "AI is dangerous," or a non-doom story twisted into fear? Second pass: does any post oversell, hype, overclaim, or run ahead of the facts? If a post hits either edge, rewrite it to the middle. The batch default should lean positive and optimistic, with at most one or two posts covering a genuinely real doom story straight if the data actually has one.

CRITICAL EXECUTION ORDER - DO NOT DEVIATE:
Step 1: Read the data files (one read_file or terminal call).
Step 2: Write all 10 posts in a single write_file call, in the four-stanza format above, each 150 to 280 chars, stanzas separated by blank lines.
Step 3: Run ONE execute_code call to verify (a) every post is 280 chars or fewer, (b) every post has at least 3 blank-line-separated stanzas, and (c) no post uses a dash as punctuation between clauses. If any fail, fix them in a single write_file overwrite. Do NOT run a second verification pass.
Step 4: Send the email with the file attached using the email-sender skill (terminal call to the SMTP script). THE EMAIL IS THE PRIMARY DELIVERABLE. SEND IT NO MATTER WHAT. Even if a post is still over 280 chars, send the email anyway. Do not let character verification block the email.
Step 5: Your final response must be ONLY "Social media questions are ready."

HARD RULES:
- You may call execute_code AT MOST 2 times total. After that, proceed to email regardless.
- The email MUST be sent. It is non-negotiable. If you are unsure whether posts fit, send the email anyway. Never skip the email.
- Do NOT loop. If a post is over 280 after your one fix, send the email with it as-is. Do not keep re-verifying.
- Never ship a batch of one-line 190-char blurbs again. That format was rejected as generic.
- Do NOT claim the email was sent unless you actually ran the SMTP script and it returned success. If the email fails, say so honestly in your final response.
